PCA is great because it effectively extracts factors based on common co-movement, the structure of how things move together. It's purely focused on that second moment information on the variance. That's a really probing question and it gets right to the heart of estimation risk. The key here is that we're not trying to perfectly predict the future sharp ratio. That's impossible. That's a great analogy. But before we get there, let's establish why the standard approach fails. What's the weak spot in a standard machine learning forecast? The fundamental vulnerability, it really lies in induction. Machine learning models are brilliant at extrapolating complex patterns from the past, but because they're purely inductive, they're just looking backwards. Exactly. They are philosophically bound to suffer performance degradation when sudden large shifts happen. Shifts they've never seen before. They're great at telling you what's likely to happen if the world keeps behaving like it just has. So, if the patterns they learned yesterday are suddenly irrelevant today, the predictions are basically useless. That's the heart of the problem. We have a few technical terms for this. First, there's non-stationerity. It just means the statistical properties of the data change over time. A correlation that held true for 5 years might just flip when the Fed changes its policy. And on top of that, financial data has a notoriously low signal to noise ratio. It's hard enough to find a signal in stable times, let alone when everything is shifting. And when that instability hits, the models run into two specific problems, two types of drift. They do, and they are lethal to profitability. The first is data drift. That's a change in the distribution of the input variables themselves. So maybe oil volatility suddenly triples. That's data drift. But the more dangerous one I think is concept drift. That's when the fundamental relationship between the input and the output changes completely. So for example, for a decade maybe low interest rates meant banks could easily lend more. That's relationship A. But then suddenly a new regulation means low rates don't increase lending. The concept has drifted. the old rules just don't apply, right? The model knows the old rules perfectly, but it can't adapt to the new ones on the fly. That feels like a perfect description of what happened in 2022. And the standard defenses, things like stop- losses or performance monitoring, they're all reactive. They wait for the model to start losing money before they kick in. Exactly. But when the shift is as fast and as large as it was in 2022, you need foresight, not a stop-loss. And that's why that year was the ultimate test. It wasn't a gentle curve. It was a complete regime change. Let's get into the details of that shift, particularly for the European markets this research focuses on. What made 2022 so different? The defining feature was the complete and the rapid reversal of monetary policy. For years, we'd had quantitative easing QE and the zero interest rate policy. Yes, it dominated the entire financial landscape. Central banks were this buyer of last resort and it distorted pricing everywhere. In 2022, the Fed, the Bank of England, and especially the European Central Bank, the ECB, they just abruptly ended it all. And the numbers from that time are pretty staggering. They really show the speed of it all. EU inflation shot up to 10% 10, which was just miles away from their 2% target. So, the ECB responded by catapulting interest rates from 0 to two and a half% in just six months. Wow. And then you add the geopolitical shock, the war in Ukraine which hit European energy supplies hard. You have a real cocktail of instability. You can see it so clearly in the bond market. The 10-year German government bond yield, a core benchmark, right? It had been negative for four years and then in 2022 it just skyrocketed. It went back to levels we hadn't seen in a decade. That's not just noise. That's a structural break. And that break had a profound effect on trader behavior. Think about it. A mid-senior trader in 2021 might have spent their entire career, say 10 years in that QE environment. Their whole intuition, their feel for the market. It was all built on a world of near zero rates. That intuition became irrelevant almost overnight. And the data itself, the actual market behavior confirmed this shift. The research looked at indices like the SXXP and the DAX. Correct. And the analysis was clear. In 2022, downtrends were much more persistent. They lasted longer. They went deeper than in the years just before 2019 to 2021. So any model trained on that recent relatively calm history would have learned that every dip gets bought up quickly was structurally unprepared for what came next. Which brings us to the centaur solution. This idea of the human as a critical editor, not a competitor to the machine. Where does that centaur name come from? It's inspired by Gary Kasparov's advanced chess. After he lost to Deep Blue in 97, Kasparov had this insight. He realized the future wasn't humans versus machines, but humans with machines. He saw that average chess players, when paired with a good computer, could often beat the most powerful supercomputers playing alone. And that gives us that fantastic quote, weak human plus machine plus better process is greater than a strong machine. So the secret ingredient isn't just raw power, it's the process. Exactly. The process of integration. The human's value isn't speed, it's judgment and domain knowledge. And in trading, this means moving the human intervention to the very beginning of the pipeline, data set selection. So, how does that play out in the 2022 scenario? When does the expert step in? In late 2021, the expert didn't need a complex signal to know trouble was brewing. They were just reading headlines, seeing the fundamental indicators. The Fed was talking about ending its bond buying. The ECB was sounding more and more hawkish. The experts hypothesis was simple. The environment ahead is going to be about rising rates and tightening liquidity. And if that's your hypothesis, then you realize the most recent data, say from 2016 to 2020, is actually toxic. It's tainted. It's not just tainted, it's actively misleading. Training on that period would teach the AI to assume central banks will always be there to suppress volatility. The human expert looks at that data and just rejects it. Throws it out completely. So where do they look instead? If the recent past is the wrong place to look, what's the right analog? The expert has to find a period in history that shares the key structural characteristics of the world they expect to see in 2022. And the period they pinpointed was 2011 to 2015. That seems counterintuitive. Why is 2011 to 2015, the era of the sovereign debt crisis, a better proxy for 2022 than say 2020? That's the core insight of the whole architecture. While 2011 to 2015 was messy, unstable, it had two crucial features that vanished later. First, interest rates while they were falling were still positive. They were non zero. Credit risk still meant something. And second, central banks while they were supportive were not doing the kind of massive open-ended QE that completely took over the later part of the decade. Ah, so the market patterns from 2011 to 2015 were formed under more, let's say, financially disciplined conditions than the Qi free-for-all. The expert is basically telling the machine, forget the last few years of funny money. This new world is going to feel more like a time when money wasn't free. That's it. Exactly. The human provides the judgment that data from a decade ago is more salient, more structurally relevant than data from yesterday. That choice is the critical human input. The AI still does all the heavy lifting, finding patterns within that curated data set, and that's what makes it true hybrid intelligence. Okay, so let's get to the results. Did this human foresight actually translate into profitability in 2022? This is where the paper makes its most powerful point. They ran simulations comparing three different trading strategies. Two were purely automatic, trained on the most recent data as you'd normally do. The third was the centaur guided strategy. Okay. So, what happened to the standard models, the ones that just learned from the recent past, those models trained on say 2016 to 2020 or 2017 to 2021, they were lossmaking across the board. They failed the stress test spectacularly because they were trained for a world that, you know, just didn't exist anymore. Give us the numbers. How bad was the damage for the SXXP index? The standard models lost between about 7.8% and 9.8%. But losses were even more severe on the German DAX. There they went as high as -6.6% P&L. These models just kept buying the dips and the dips just kept getting deeper all year. A really tough year for pure automation. So now the moment of truth. What about the Centaur strategy? The one trained on that older but more relevant data from 2011 2015. The human-guided approach, it significantly outperformed both of the automated ones. For the SXXP index, that curated strategy translated the learned patterns into a profitable year. It generated a P&L of over 11.6%. Wait, let's just pause on that for a second. That's a performance swing of over 20 percentage points compared to the worst automated model. One model loses nearly 10%. The hybrid model gains almost 12. That's the difference between a successful fund and having to explain things to your clients. It really is. It highlights the sheer leverage of getting the data selection right. And even on the DAX, which was an incredibly difficult market that year, the curated strategy still provided massive risk mitigation where the automated models lost up to 16%, the Centaur model limited losses to just 5.6%. So even when it couldn't find a profit, the human intervention prevented a catastrophe. Absolutely. The takeaway is just so powerful. When you face a paradigm shift, the model trained on older but more salient data just blows away the models trained on the most recent but misleading history. The machine's power is useless if the human points it at the wrong map. And this just solidifies the argument that this is the future. this convergence of discretionary human judgment and quantitative power. The expert's unique skill is validating the knowledge base. And we don't have to look far to see the dangers of not doing this. You mentioned a great realworld example earlier, Zillow. The implosion of their eye buying program Zillow offers in late 2021. Right. Zillow lost billions and shut the business down. And it wasn't because their pricing algorithm was weak. It was a concept drift problem. That's the clear implication. Their algorithms were being fed all this data from the peak pandemic housing boom, a totally anomalous period. And the failure was the absence of a human intervention, an internal centaur to step in and say, "Stop. This pandemic data is not a normal baseline for what comes next." The inputs were just structurally irrelevant. And the automated predictions failed catastrophically. It just reinforces the thesis of the research. It does. The issue isn't the algorithm. It's the relevance of the data. Neural networks are amazing pattern detectors, but if the knowledge base is not strictly relevant, the results are bound to be sub-optimal. This is why you see this hybrid idea taking hold. Good forecasters have always done this manually, drawing historical parallels. The centaur architecture just bakes that skill into the automated pipeline. Now, we focused entirely on the human empowering the AI at the start of the process, defining the knowledge base before the model runs. Yes, positioning the expert at the front of the pipeline. And that leaves us with a final provocative thought for you to mle over. The decisive factor really seems to be the human defining the scope of the machine's knowledge and then judging if that knowledge is fit for purpose. It's not about computation, it's about context.

Okay, let's set the scene before we get into the machine learning part. Maybe a quick history lesson. Where did this all start? I guess the capital asset pricing model, right? CAPM back in the 60s. The idea is elegant, wasn't it? Your expected return above, like a safety bill depends only on how much your stock moves with the overall market. Beta was king. Simple, intuitive. But it didn't take long for cracks to appear. Researchers started finding things, these anomalies that CAPM just couldn't explain. You had the value effect, cheaper stocks doing better, right? And the size effect smaller companies outperforming. These findings really started to undermine the simplicity of CAPM. They showed market beta wasn't the whole story. Not even close really. And that led to the next big era, multiffactor models. Building on theory, people started looking for other systematic risks. And this is where FMA and French had their huge impact in 93. They basically said, "Look, these value and size effects, they seem persistent. Maybe they represent risk factors, too." So they added two factors to the market beta. HML for value, SMB for size. And they built these factors using real portfolio data. You know, going long highv value stocks and short low value, long small stocks and short big ones. This three factor model. It became the new benchmark. Explain returns much better for a while anyway. Exactly. For a while. But then history repeated itself. Hundreds of new anomalies started popping up. Things the three-factor model couldn't explain either. The most famous one probably being momentum stocks that go up tend to keep going up for a bit. And that kicked off the multiffactor model wars in the 2010s, didn't it? People were proposing new models. FMA and French came back with five factors. How and colleagues had four. Everyone was trying to explain this growing zoo of anomalies. But interestingly, FMA and French themselves pointed out something critical later on. This difference between static models where factor exposures are fixed, right? Versus dynamic or conditional models where things like a company's size or value exposure could change over time. and the dynamic models just work better consistently, which kind of hints that maybe trying to pin down fixed factors wasn't the whole story precisely. And that realization coincided perfectly with this explosion in data. We entered the era of well, highdimensional covariants, hundreds, potentially thousands of things that might predict returns. We're not just talking about the usual price and accounting data anymore. Now we have this wave of alternative data. Okay, so what kind of stuff are we talking about? Oh, all sorts. Things like aggregated trading account data from brokers lets you see what retail investors are doing collectively, though it's often private. Then there's super granular order book data showing millisecond by millisecond supply and demand. Wow. What else? Crowdsourced data. Think employee reviews on glass door predicting company performance or data from mobile apps tracking user engagement or even investor opinions. Then there's textual data. Machine learning is reading through financial reports, looking for changes in language that predict returns, analyzing news articles, even patent filings to map out technological links between firms. And believe it or not, image data, analyzing the sentiment of photos in news articles about a company, or using ML to spot patterns in candlestick charts, the kind of technical analysis traders have done by eye for years, but now automated and scaled up. It's incredible the range of inputs. And you mentioned this interesting trade-off with analyst forecasts and alternative data. Yeah, that was a fascinating study. It seems alternative data helps analysts make better short-term forecasts, probably because they get information quicker, cheaper, but it might actually hurt their long-term accuracy. How come? The idea is limited attention. Analysts get swamped by the short-term noise from all this fast data, and maybe, just maybe, they lose focus on the bigger, slower moving picture. So, the accuracy curve gets steeper, better now, worse later. And it's not always about super exotic data. Sometimes it's just connecting existing data in new ways. Alternative like data. Think economic links like supply chains. Exactly. Supply chains, shared customers, industry relationships. If firm A is a major supplier to firm B, news about firm A should affect firm B, right? But maybe investors don't react instantly. This creates lead lag effects. We've seen studies like in the Chinese market showing you could earn pretty significant returns by exploiting these links assuming investors underreact or are just slow to process these spillovers. And what about mutual funds? Right? Mutual fund implied information. Two main types. First, just looking at what funds hold. The idea is that fund managers collectively have some skill or insight. Their aggregate holdings might tell you something. Second, looking at fund flows where investor money is moving. When money flows into certain funds, it can push up the prices of the stocks they hold and vice versa. This can create predictable patterns in prices and fund returns. So, we have this absolute mountain of data now. Traditional, alternative, linked. But that creates its own problem, doesn't it? How do you even figure out the relationships? They must be getting incredibly complex. That's the core challenge. The relationship between all these potential predictors and actual returns is well, elusive. We don't know the true model for valuing a stock. We don't know exactly how investors use all this information which leads to model uncertainty. Precisely. Some research suggests that basically all these hundreds of factors might have some chance of being in the true model. There isn't one single perfect specification waiting to be found. So if you just pick a few factors you like and ignore the rest, you're probably missing something. Ignoring that uncertainty, imposing what we call sparcity, assuming only a few things matter, could mean leaving real investment opportunities on the table. And it's not just which factors matter, but how they interact. You mentioned nonlinearity. Yes, exactly. Relationships aren't always straight lines. Think about how the economy affects stocks. It's not always linear. Transaction costs can create nonlinear effects. Investor behavior overreacting, underreacting, that's definitely not linear. Often the real juice is in the interactions between factors, not just the factors themselves. Maybe momentum works differently for value stocks versus growth stocks or in different market conditions. Traditional methods really struggle to find these complex interactive nonlinear patterns. Okay. So this complexity, this model uncertainty, this nonlinearity, it sounds like the old ways of doing things were hitting a wall. They were. And this is where Leo Brimman's idea of the two cultures in statistics become so relevant to finance. Right. explain that. Okay, so culture one is the data modeling culture. That's traditional econometrics. You start by assuming a probabilistic model generates the data. The goal is to understand the structure, estimate the parameters of that assumed model, maybe infer causality. Getting unbiased estimates is key and culture too. That's the algorithmic modeling culture. That's machine learning. Here, the process is treated more like a black box. The absolute priority is predictive accuracy. How well does the model work on new data it hasn't seen before? It uses datadriven methods, lets the data guide the model structure, handles complexity, nonlinearity, high dimensions naturally. The goal is minimizing out of sample prediction errors. So putting it simply, econometrics prioritizes understanding the parameters while machine learning prioritizes predictive power. That's a great summary. Parameter estimation versus predictive accuracy. It's a fundamental difference in philosophy. Okay, so let's connect this philosophical shift to actual strategies and results. How does ML tackle the problems we discussed like too many variables? Well, traditional methods choke on high dimensionality. Too many variables cause issues like multiolinearity, makes models unstable, prone to overfitting. So they often resort to sparity assumptions, deliberately picking only a few factors, which as you said might miss important information. Exactly. It means a potential loss of investment opportunities. Plus practically how do you do the traditional portfolio sorting if you have say 50 potential factors it becomes impossible. So how do the results compare? The difference is pretty stark especially out of sample. If you look at sharp ratios a measure of riskadjusted return traditional factor models like the FMA French three factor might get you say 6 maybe up to 1.8 for newer ones but the machine learning models recent studies show sharp ratios hitting 2.4 2.8 8 even over three consistently out of sample. That's a huge leap. Wow. And why the big difference? Because ML models can handle all those coariantss. They use techniques like regularization to prevent overfitting, but they don't have to throw away potentially useful information by imposing sparsity beforehand. And the models that allow factor exposures to change over time, the conditional models, they tend to do even better. It really suggests that trying to find the small set of static factors might have been well maybe not the most fruitful path for maximizing prediction. Machine learning also changes how you even form portfolios to test models, right? Instead of just sorting into simple buckets. Yeah. Methods like asset pricing trees are interesting. They use decision tree logic to group assets in much more complex datadriven ways, specifically designed to maximize the explanatory power for returns. They capture way more cross-sectional information than simple sorting. And what about choosing the factors themselves or dealing with irrelevant ones? ML offers tools there too. Things like lasso regression can automatically select the most predictive variables from a huge list, effectively shrinking the impact of irrelevant ones. Or techniques like principal component analysis, PCA, can distill hundreds of correlated variables into a smaller set of underlying latent factors that capture the most important information. Okay. But with all this power and flexibility comes a risk, right? Overfitting, making models that are too complex. Absolutely. That's a key challenge. If you just throw complex ML algorithms at financial data without care, you will overfit. The model will look amazing on past data but fall apart on future data. That's why regularization is non-negotiable. It's a set of techniques that penalize model complexity, forcing the model to focus on the most robust patterns and improve its generalization to new data. But then there's this really weird idea, the double descent. Ah yes that's fascinating and kind of counterintuitive. The traditional view is model complexity increases error goes down then it hits a sweet spot then error goes back up due to overfitting. Double descent suggests that if you keep making the model even more complex pushing into what's called the overparameterized regime where you have more parameters than data points the generalization error can actually start to decrease again. Seriously more complexity becomes good again potentially. Yes. It's like there's a second valley of good performance way out in the complexity landscape. This has led to research on the virtue of complexity in finance. Studies are finding that sometimes these hugely complex models like deep neural networks with tons of parameters can actually achieve better out of sample performance and asset pricing than simpler models. It's still an active area of research, but it challenges our old intuitions about overfitting. Okay, let's address the elephant in the room, the blackbox problem. If these models are so complex, how do we know why they're making certain predictions? Isn't interpretability important? It's hugely important, especially in finance and academia. And yes, some ML models can be black boxes, but it's not always the case, and there's a lot of work being done on interpretability. Can you give example? Sure. Researchers using PCA find the main components often correspond closely to familiar factors like value and momentum. Other methods like instrumented PCA show factors that look like portfolios managed based on characteristics. Techniques like permutation importance can tell you which input variables the model relies on most and often. It highlights things like momentum, liquidity, risk measures that decades of research have pointed to or analyzing the weights in the model can reveal which economic forces like transaction frictions or value concepts are driving the predictions. So we are finding ways to peak inside the box. So where does this leave us? How do we tie all this together? One powerful way is through the lens of the stochastic discount factor or SDF. Okay, the SDF. Explain that. Think of the SDF as a kind of universal pricing kernel. It's a theoretical concept MT + 1 that relates today's price to tomorrow's expected payoff adjusted for risk. You can write it as a function of asset returns specifically like MT + 1 equals 1 minus some weighted combination of excess returns. The key insight is that the weights in this combination can be seen as a function of firm characteristics, size, value, momentum, all that stuff we talked about. And crucially, this function can be complex, nonlinear. So the SDF framework can handle both old and new. Exactly. It's broad enough to encompass traditional models like FMA French where the weights are basically determined by portfolio sorts. And these new machine learning approaches where the relationship between characteristics and the SDF weights is learned directly from the data potentially in a very complex nonlinear way. It allows the way we construct factors or manage portfolios to be much more sophisticated. So if you want to build the best predictive model within this framework, what are the key steps? It really boils down to three things all aimed at maximizing that out of sample sharp ratio. Selecting the characteristics, the C's, which variables actually predict returns. This involves careful feature selection, maybe using ML techniques themselves. Constructing the managed portfolios, the FS, how do you combine those characteristics into factors or trading signals? This is moving from simple sorts to more advanced, possibly MLdriven highdimensional sorting, estimating the SDF coefficients, the E. How much do investors actually care about the risks associated with these factors? This involves statistical estimation, crucially using regularization to make sure the estimates are robust and work out of sample. Okay, that sounds like a plan. But what are the pitfalls, the downsides? It can't be easy. Definitely not easy. The biggest challenge is still the fundamental nature of financial data. It has very low signal to noise ratio. Finding the true predictive patterns amidst all the randomness is incredibly hard. Plus, markets change. Relationships aren't stable. There's a lack of stationerity. What worked last year might not work next year. This means you can't just plug financial data into standard off-the-shelf machine learning algorithms and expect miracles. So you need more than just the algorithm. Absolutely. You need to integrate economic theory and financial intuition using Beijian methods that incorporate prior beliefs, building in constraints based on economic reasoning. These things are crucial for guiding the ML models and ensuring the results are sensible and robust, not just statistical artifacts. And we always have to remember the no free lunch theorem. different ML models, different choices of variables, different regularization techniques. These all represent different implicit assumptions or priors about how markets work. They will lead to different results. There's no single magic bullet, which is a good warning against just, you know, torturing the data until it confesses. Exactly. Avoid model hacking or P hacking. The goal isn't just finding something that worked in the past, but building models with genuine predictive power, ideally grounded in some economic understanding. So wrapping this up, we've seen a real journey from simple models trying to explain past returns driven by theory to this new world of big data and machine learning intensely focused on maximizing future predictive accuracy. Right? ML gives us the tools to handle the sheer scale and complexity of modern financial data to find those subtle nonlinear patterns. But it's not magic. It needs to be guided by economic reasoning to be truly effective and interpretable. It's a fascinating blend of disciplines. Really, it is. It's an ongoing evolution combining the rigor of economics with the power of computer science and statistics. Okay. So, here's a final thought for you, our listeners. Look at recent correlations. So Chernov, Dquist, and Lockto in that 2025 paper show how you can use standard econometric tools to estimate the conditional mean variance and correlations and actually build a candidate MVE portfolio and sovereign bonds too. Ah, good question. They have to test it. There's a statistical test called the Gibbons, Ross, and Shanken tests. the GRS test. It basically checks if the portfolio they constructed could statistically be the one with the maximal sharp ratio among all possible combinations of those assets. And did these currency and bond MVEs pass? They did. Yeah. Since you can't easily build the MV directly, the goal shifts. Then you use that hedge portfolio to neutralize the unpriced risk in your main factor portfolio. How do they build these hedge portfolios? Sounds tricky. There are a few different methodologies researchers are exploring. Some look at how coariances relate to characteristics. Daniel, Moda, Rodki, and Santos proposed a clever double sorting method, sorting stocks first on a characteristic, then on their co-variance with that characteristic factor to try and isolate the unpriced bet. Others like Herskovich, Morera, and Mure use single sorting on betas relative to certain factors. It represents pure time preference, you know, how patient capital is, or as we'll explore a bit later, international capital flows. Okay. But the mechanism of how these three shocks interact with the stock market is where the entire traditional finance model just falls apart. Why is that? Because growth shocks and risk shocks have a remarkably messy and often negative transmission to equity valuations. They don't boost stocks cleanly at all. Let's break down the mechanics of that messy transmission because why wouldn't a rate drop driven by a growth shock help my portfolio? Well, think about how stocks are actually valued. A stock's price is determined by its future cash flows divided by a discount rate. Right. So, if interest rates fall because the economy's expected growth just collapsed, your discount rate goes down, which is good. Right. Lower denominator. But the collapse in growth means the company's future cash flows, the numerator in that equation, are also going to collapse. Oh, I see. So, those two dynamics are just fighting each other. Exactly. And often, the terrible economic growth heavily outweighs the benefit of the lower interest rate, so the stock price actually drops. It's like looking at a friend who just lost 20 lb. Okay. I like where this is going. You can't just run up and congratulate them. Right. You have to ask how they lost it. Did they lose 20 lb of fat? Right. be a pure discounting shock, which is great. Or did they lose like muscle mass and bone density? Because that would be a drop in expected growth, Right. which is obviously really bad. You have to know what they lost before you know if it's healthy. That analogy maps perfectly to the math because if the interest rate drops due to a pure discounting shock, the fat loss in your analogy, that is the only shock that transmits one-for-one to stock prices. Because it doesn't touch the earnings. Right. Pure discounting doesn't touch the company's underlying cash flows. So, a 1% drop in the pure discount rate mechanically gives equity valuations a clean 1% boost. Wow. But if rates drop because of muscle loss, a deteriorating economic outlook, stocks do not get that mechanical lift. Okay, so if pure discounting is the only force giving a clean boost to stock prices, we need to apply this to the last three decades of market data. Yeah, let's look at the reality. Right. Like, does isolating the fat from the muscle actually solve this stock yield disconnect. It solves it almost entirely. When the authors strip away the noise of growth and risk, and they look solely at the pure discounting term, it explains 80% of cross-country valuation changes across the G7 economies since 1990. 80%? That's massive. It's huge. The disconnect basically vanishes, and the relationship between pure discount rates and stock valuations becomes effectively a straight line. Imagine giving an AI just a handful of standard accounting variables, locking it in a digital sandbox, and coming back a few hours later to find out it has independently reconstructed like 50 years of Nobel Prize-winning financial theory. Yeah, I mean, it's a completely profound shift. We're moving from AI as just this processor of existing text, you know, to an engine of genuine scientific discovery. Right. And when you apply that leap to modern finance, specifically asset pricing, the stakes get incredibly high, and well, the methods have to be absolutely bulletproof. Exactly. And that is what we are exploring in this deep dive. We're looking at a pretty groundbreaking piece of research from April 2026. It's titled Can AI do financial research? LLM-guided hypothesis discovery in asset pricing. And the authors are this powerhouse team of researchers from Google, Boston College, Columbia, and Cheung Kong GSB. But, you know, our mission today isn't just to see if the AI pulled this off. Right, that's just the surface level. Yeah, we want to understand how it thinks. How does it react when its ideas completely fail? And what happens when its discoveries are put through, like, the absolute most brutal statistical filters in modern finance? It's a gauntlet. It really is. And ironically, it turns out that putting extremely strict constraints on an AI is precisely what breeds its creativity. Thank you for tuning in to Quantopian's Quant Radio, your AI-driven podcast exploring everything related to quantitative finance. If you enjoyed this episode, don't forget to like and subscribe to stay updated on future releases. For more Quant-focused content, join us at community.quantopian.com. There you can explore a wealth of resources, connect with fellow quants, engage in insightful discussions, and enhance your skills through our extensive range of online courses. Quant Radio is intended to help people develop their knowledge and skills in Quant finance. This podcast is not intended to provide investment advice. And now, back to the episode. I think the word constraints is the perfect place to start because it's really easy to imagine this experiment as just, you know, letting a large language model loose on a Bloomberg terminal. Oh, yeah, just scraping the internet and throwing darts at ticker symbols based on the news. Exactly. But, that is not what happened here. The researchers built a highly rigorous, controlled laboratory environment. The AI is simply the agent operating inside of it. Okay, let's unpack this because the researchers didn't just tell Claude Opus 4.6 to go make money. No, definitely not. They designed what they actually call a signal laboratory. It's effectively a mathematical sandbox. Yeah. And inside the sandbox, they gave the AI a really specific set of primitives. Right, the building blocks. Exactly. There are exactly 66 standard Compustat accounting variables. So, things like total assets, long-term debt, R&D expense, cost of goods sold. Yeah. And then, they gave it exactly 24 mathematical operators. So, functions like growth, ADD, moving average, or industry adjustment. And it's a highly constrained symbolic grammar. Like, the AI cannot just write arbitrary, convoluted Python code to figure this out. Right. It's forced to combine these specific variables using these specific operators up to a maximum nesting depth of six. So, it's entirely bounded by the actual language of fundamental accounting. It honestly reminds me of a cooking competition show, like Chopped. Oh, that's a good way to look at it. Right. The human researchers are the judges. They provide a highly specific pantry, the 66 variables, and they provide the kitchen equipment, which is the 24 operators. But, the AI is the chef. The AI has to figure out how to combine those raw ingredients into a recipe that actually works. Or in this case, a financial signal that predicts returns. What's fascinating here is why the researchers imposed those pantry rules in the first place, to borrow your analogy. In traditional machine learning applied to finance, you usually get a black box. Because if you submit a maker order, you might just sit in the book and miss the jump entirely. So, you have to be a taker, and takers pay fees. Exactly the problem. On Hyperliquid, the specific exchange where this data is from, the taker fee ranges from 1.44 to 2.7 basis points per trade. Oh, the math completely falls apart. If my expected profit from reading the invisible tea leaves is 0.2 basis points, but I have to pay the exchange 2.0 basis points just to execute the immediate trade, you lose money every single time you push the button. The profits are so incredibly thin that they are completely swallowed by the structural fees if you try to exploit this via simple directional taker strategies. So, the only people who can actually use this predictive signal are the hyper-optimized algorithms that are already playing that intense queue priority game we talked about earlier. The ones running at the locked door. Exactly. The ones who can magically slip their orders in as makers the millisecond the door unlocks, avoiding the fee altogether. It is a game of pennies played at the speed of light that only the most heavily capitalized and technologically advanced firms can participate in. They are fighting for fractions of a basis point, and they are doing it by generating $3 a minute in error codes. It's unbelievable. It's an ecosystem of pure friction that exists completely out of sight. That is just wild. It's a whole invisible ecosystem functioning right underneath the surface of the charts and graphs we all look at on our screens. Yeah, it's a lot to process. High frequency traders are essentially spamming cryptocurrency markets to get in line first. They are running full speed at the locked door. This physical reality results in billions of dollars of invisible, mechanically rejected orders every single minute. Yet, because these rejections represent the true underlying intent of the smartest algorithms in the market, the latent signal, the umbrellas opening, they actually predict the future twice as well as the visible data everyone else is looking at. And the realization that intent is more predictive than execution is profound. Whenever you look at data, whether it's at work in a quarterly report, in the political news, or just in your own personal finances, you have to remember to separate the cause from the symptom. Just because two things happen together doesn't mean one caused the other. Sometimes the thing you think is the cause is actually just a symptom of a deeper hidden signal that you aren't seeing.

So, let's peel this back because I think for a lot of people, correlation and causation, they just get lumped together. They do. We all took stats 101. We know correlation does not imply causation, but in practice, if X moves with Y, we assume they're linked. Why is that so dangerous here? Let's use the analogy the authors borrow from Clive Granger, the Nobel laurate. It's a classic, but it perfectly illustrates the trap. Imagine a rooster on a farm. Every single morning, without fail, the rooster crows and a few minutes later, the sun rises. All right. So, if I'm running a regression analysis, my model says the rooster is a perfect predictor of sunrise. Exactly. High statistical significance, high predictive power. If you just want to know when the sun will rise, listening for the rooster is a perfectly valid strategy. That's association. But investing isn't passive. No, investing is an intervention. You aren't just watching the sun. You're trying to act on the market. If you confuse association for causation, you might think, well, if I make the rooster crow at 2 a.m., the sun will rise, which is obviously absurd. But translate that to stocks. Well, the paper argues this is exactly what factor investors do. They see that stocks with, say, high asset growth tend to have low returns. That's the rooster. They assume the growth causes the low returns, so they short those stocks. But if there isn't a causal link, if they're just two things happening together for some third unseen reason, then the strategy falls apart. you're betting on a mechanism that doesn't exist. So the standard tools we use, OS, linear regression, maximizing R squar, they are essentially just rooster detectors. In a way, yes, the math doesn't care why the numbers line up. And in fact, the standard academic approach, the three pass regression, actually incentivizes researchers to just add more and more variables to get a better fit. You're just stuffing the model. We're stuffing it with roosters. And this brings us to the core technical argument of the paper. There are two specific ways this goes wrong. Two villains, if you will. The confounder and the collider. Okay, let's start with the confounder. This one feels a little more intuitive to me. It's the omitted variable. Right. Correct. A confounder is a third variable that's driving both your factor and your returns. A classic example in finance is leverage. Walk me through that. Okay. Say you're looking at the booktomarket ratio. that cheap stocks, high booktomarket have high returns. You think, great, I found the value premium. Buy cheap stocks, get rich, standard value investing. But hang on, what if distressed companies that are about to go bust have low stock prices? That gives them a high book to market. Okay, I'm with you. And what if those same distressed companies also have to offer higher returns to convince people to hold their risky debt or equity? Ah, so the risk is actually coming from the distress, the leverage, not the value factor itself. Exactly. Leverage is the confounder. It causes both the cheap price and the high return. If you build a model that ignores leverage, you think you're buying value, but you're actually just loading up on bankruptcy risks. You're attributing the return to the wrong thing, to the wrong driver. That makes sense. You missed a variable, so your map is incomplete. Yeah, but that seems solvable. Just add leverage to the model, right? In theory, yes. If you identify the confounder and control for it, you can fix the bias. But the paper spends way more time on the second villain, the collider. They call it the false friend. And this concept is a lot harder to wrap your head around because it defies our instinct to be thorough. Okay. False friend sounds ominous. Give me the definition. A collider is a variable that is the result, the effect of both your factor and the return. It happens downstream in the causal chain. Okay, I'm going to need a concrete example here. My brain is trying to picture this. Let's stick with stocks. Imagine you have a factor, let's say book tomarket again, and you have future returns. Got it? The analyst looks at the stock's valuation, the booktomarket, and they also look at its expected returns. Sure, both of those things matter. So the analyst rating is caused by both the factor and the return. It's a collider. It collides the two inputs into one output. Okay, I follow. The rating is the child of the other two variables. And here is the trap. In standard stats, we're taught to control for things. We think, I want to isolate the signal, so I'll control for the analyst rating. But when you control for a collider, you open this logical back door. You create a statistical correlation between booktomarket and returns that doesn't actually exist in reality. Wait, explain that. How does looking at the rating create a fake connection? This is the part that always trips me up. Okay, think of it like this. Now, if a stock in that neutral pile has really high returns, but the analyst still only rated it neutral, what must be true about its book to market to keep the rating that low? Oh, I see. If the returns were good, the rating should have been higher. So, if it's still stuck at neutral, something must be pelling it down. So, the book to market must be terrible. Bingo. By forcing the rating to be constant, you've made it so that if one variable goes up, the other must go down to compensate. You've mathematically forced a relationship. You created a correlation out of thin air just by sorting the data. So the variables might have zero relationship in the wild. But because I sorted them by the analyst rating, I suddenly see a pattern. Precisely. That correlation is the mirage and the kicker. Including that collider often makes your model look better on paper. Your R squ goes up. Your P values look incredibly significant because you've successfully modeled the artificial relationship. you just created. Yes, you're patting yourself on the back for finding a pattern that you effectively hallucinated. And the worst part is you can't trade it. Why not? If the pattern is there in the data because by the time you observe the collider, by the time the analyst rating is published, the return it was based on has already happened. You are essentially using information from the future to predict the past. So it works in a back test, but in real time trading, you can't see the future. You can't. That is yeah actually terrifying for a data scientist. It means better stats can equal worse reality. That's completely counterintuitive. And that's the central warning. Basically, a piece of software that maps out cause and effect without human bias, right? And what they found was growth models that were completely backward. Today we are tackling a real corporate finance mystery. Something that was for all intents and purposes dead and buried. We're talking about the stock split. It's this maneuver where a company basically slices its shares into smaller cheaper pieces. So one share worth $1,000 might become say 10 shares worth $100 each. And for over a decade it was considered almost obsolete, an artifact of a different time in the market. If you look at the numbers, splits were just in a freef fall after 2000 and they hit this incredible low point of just six splits in 2009. Exactly. The reasons for their decline were solid. And yet all of a sudden, we see these huge high-profile tech firms, Apple, Tesla, Amazon, Google, they're all doing it again. Which brings us to the central puzzle. I mean, if you, the listener, can just log into your trading app right now and buy a fractional share, a tiny piece of a $3,000 Amazon stock, why on earth would Amazon bother splitting it? The old logic just doesn't hold up. And that is our mission for this deep dive. We're here to unpack a new theory that the modern stock split isn't what it used to be. It's no longer just about trading mechanic. It's evolved. It's now this powerful what the research calls a dualpurpose attention catalyst. a dualpurpose catalyst, meaning it's designed to attract not just investors, but and this is the key part, customers as well. Thank you for tuning in to Quantopian's Quant Radio, your AI-driven podcast exploring everything related to quantitative finance. If you enjoy this episode, don't forget to like and subscribe to stay updated on future releases. For more quant focused content, join us at community.quantopian.com. There you can explore a wealth of resources, connect with fellow quants, engage in insightful discussions, and enhance your skills through our extensive range of online courses. Quant radio is intended to help people develop their knowledge and skills in quant finance. This podcast is not intended to provide investment advice. And now back to the episode. Yeah. And to really get it, we have to go back to the beginning. We need to understand the old world, the traditional reasons for splitting a stock. Okay, let's do that. So before this practice nearly died out, what was the standard rationale? Why would a company do this 2530 years ago? Well, there were two big ideas. The first and most common one was something called the trading range or the anchoring hypothesis. Anchoring. So like a psychological thing. Exactly. The thinking was that there's a sort of comfortable price range for a stock, maybe between 20 and $100. If it got much higher than that, it just felt too expensive for the average retail investor. Even if they could afford it, the sticker price was off-putting, right? It was basically a marketing move to keep the price looking attractive. The second idea was what's called theformational signaling hypothesis. Okay? Signaling what? Confidence. Splitting a stock isn't free, it's a hassle. So when management announced a split, they were essentially telling the market, "We are so confident in our future growth that this stock is going to be right back up at $1,000 soon. So we're splitting it now." And there's data to back that up, right? That it was a positive signal. Oh, absolutely. Studies found that historically split stocks tended to outperform the market by about 8% or even more in the year after the split. So it was a credible costly signal of financial health. But then the world changed. Our source material points to a couple of huge shifts that really just eroded those reasons. The first one was the rise of institutional ownership. You know, huge mutual funds, pension funds, hedge funds. They started to dominate trading. And they don't care if a stock is $50 or $5,000. Not at all. They're trading in massive blocks and have the capital. The psychological appeal to the little guy just mattered less and less. And the second shift, which is more on the technical side, was decimalization, right? A huge one. In 2001, US markets switched from pricing stocks in fractions like eighs and 16s to decimals, which made the bid ask spread the gap between the buying and selling price much much smaller. Exactly. And that basically wiped out one of the main microructure benefits of splitting. There was just less of a financial incentive to do it. So splits declined, they nearly vanished. But then the environment changed again. And this is where we get to the turning point. 2008. The period right after the financial crisis completely transformed retail investing. This was the birth of the attention economy, but applied directly to the stock market. You've got the rise of commission free trading. Mobile apps like Robin Hood become ubiquitous. And then there's the explosion of financial talk on social media, Reddit, X, everywhere. All the friction to trading just disappeared. And suddenly the most valuable currency wasn't commissions. It was attention. And in that kind of world, a stock split is. It's like a perfect marketing event. It's low cost. It generates a ton of media coverage. It trends online. And crucially, it sends an immediate notification to millions of users on brokerage apps who have that stock on their watch list. It's a huge coordinated alert which is the engine for this dualpurpose catalyst idea. It grabs the attention of retail investors who we know are drawn to these high-profile events and it captures the attention of potential customers. Right? The research has shown for a while that high firm visibility can boost how customers see you and that can actually drive sales. The split becomes this viral moment where your company's name is just everywhere linked to this idea of success. That's a powerful theory. But, you know, proving that a stock split actually makes more people buy iPhones or shop on Amazon, that's a big claim. So, let's get into the data. What's the evidence this actually works? Okay, so first you have to show that splits still do the old job, which is improving liquidity, making the stock easier to trade. And the research confirms they absolutely do. But how do we know that's from attention and not just, you know, the lower price, making things work better mechanically? That's a great question. The research uses a couple of key indicators. First is something called the amii heard illi liquidity measure. Okay, that sounds pretty technical in plain English. What's that telling us? Think of it like this. It's measuring the cost of trading. How much does the price move? If you try to buy or sell a bunch of shares, a high score means the stock is really illquid. The price moves a lot on you. So, a lower number is what you want. Higher liquidity. A lower number is much better. And the research finds this measure drops significantly right after a split. the stock gets easier and cheaper to trade and they confirm that with the bid ask spread too. They do the spread between the bid and ask price gets significantly smaller. So yes, splits still improve liquidity. They are still attracting investor attention and trading. Okay, so that's the investor side. Now for the really new part, the customer side. If this is truly a dualpurpose catalyst, does that attention actually translate into sales? It does. And this is probably the most fascinating new finding in the research. They tracked firms quarterly net sales and they found that sales increase significantly after a stock split. That's incredible. A company makes a financial announcement and their sales go up. It's like a free advertising campaign. It's free advertising with this implied stamp of success. The buzz around the split seems to boost customer confidence and interest in the company's products. For a consumer-f facing company like an Apple or an Amazon, this isn't just a financial decision, it's a marketing one. So that brings us to the paradox then. If splits work by getting attention, who benefits the most? Is it the huge companies that are already famous or is it the smaller firms that really need the spotlight? Well, when you look at the whole sample going from 1984 to 2021, the data is pretty clear. Smaller firms and firms with less institutional ownership benefit significantly more from both the liquidity boost and the sales growth from both. Which makes perfect sense, right? If you're a small consumer tech company, a sudden blast of positive media attention from a split is going to move the needle on your sales way more than it would for a giant like Google. The relative benefit is much bigger for them. Which brings us right back to the puzzle. If that's true, why are the meggaaps, the Teslas and the Googles, the ones leading this new wave of splits? Because they're not playing the same game. They're not chasing relative gains. They are chasing the absolute volume of retail investors, acquiring new individual shareholders. Exactly. And to prove this, the research has to go deeper than standard liquidity metrics. They use this incredibly detailed trading data. It's called TAQ data. TAQ stands for trade. end quote. It's like the highest resolution X-ray you can get of trading activity. It lets you see the size and frequency of every single trade, which means you can tell the difference between a huge institutional block trade and the smaller, more frequent trades that are typical of a retail investor. Precisely. And using that data, what they find is that after a split, retail trading just explodes. Both retail buying and selling in terms of volume and frequency increase significantly. So, the split definitely pulls in the retail crowd. But here's the nuance. It doesn't pull them in equally for all firms. Not at all. This is the key. That positive increase in retail trading is significantly more pronounced for the large market cap firms and the high institutionally owned firms. So, a huge company like Apple sees its retail by frequency jump much much more than a smaller companies would. Way more. The mega caps are just exceptionally good at converting that media buzz into a massive influx of individual traders. This all points to a fundamental shift. To really see it, we have to compare the two eras directly. Pre208 versus post208. Let's start with liquidity. Before 2008, the liquidity effects were pretty strong across the board. That was kind of the main point of doing a split back then. But after 2008, in this new attention-driven world, the benefit gets much more selective. In the post208 period, the liquidity effect is only statistically significant for large firms and high institutionally owned firms. That's fascinating. So for a small company now, the liquidity argument for splitting has kind of faded away. It seems to have. I mean, with fractional shares being so common, retail traders can get in anyway, but for the big firms, the massive wave of retail attention they generate still seems to tighten their spreads and improve their trading environment. Okay. Okay, now for the customer side. If this is really about attention, the sales bump should be way stronger in the social media era. And it is. This is where the difference is just night and day. The sales growth effect is significantly more pronounced in the post208 period. Before then, it was barely even significant. The link between stock market buzz and actual sales has become incredibly tight. And who's best at capitalizing on that? Now, again, it's the large firms. In the recent period, that sales growth effect is statistically significant only for the big well-known companies. So, their brand recognition acts like a massive amplifier for the buzz created by the split. It seems so. They can convert that attention into customers more effectively than anyone else. Okay. So, speaking of buzz, let's talk about the immediate market reaction. The announcement happens. What does the research say about how investors react in the short term? The market loves it right away. If you look at that short window 3 days before to 3 days after the announcement, there's a cumulative abnormal return of about 1%. And a 1% abnormal return is significant. The market is cheering definitely, but the cheers are louder for some than for others. The short-term pop is significantly higher for small firms around 1 and a.5% and for low institutionally owned firms where it's closer to 2%. Which makes sense. For a smaller, lesserknown company, the news carries more weight. It's a stronger signal of management's confidence. Exactly. For a company like Amazon, it might only be about half a percent. The news is less surprising. What about the longer term picture? Historically, we know split stocks tended to outperform. They did. Over a 2-year period, those returns were positive, and they were mainly driven by those same small low IO firms, the ones who really needed the signal and the liquidity. But let me guess, in the post208 world, that script gets flipped too. It does. In the modern sample, the analysis shows that only large firms have statistically significant long-term positive returns. So, the market seems to be rewarding the biggest players for using this tool strategically in the new attention economy, believing they can turn that retail engagement into lasting value. It's just a completely different tool than it was 20 years ago. It's evolved from a simple mechanical fix into this complex strategic play for visibility. So to synthesize this for everyone listening, what this all means is that the return of the stock split isn't some retro trend. It's a very modern adaptation to this new social mediadriven investing world. Right? Splits are now strategic attention catalysts. They still boost liquidity, but they also drive real sales and that sales effect is much much stronger in the post208 era. And while the smaller firms might get the biggest relative bang for their buck, the mega caps, your Apples, your Amazons are splitting because they are just incredibly effective at converting that attention into a massive volume of new retail investors. Which leads us with that final really provocative question to think about. If fractional trading makes high-pric stocks accessible to everyone and the biggest relative gains go to the smaller firms, why are these massive institutionally owned companies making this a priority? And the research offers a really compelling possibility that the value they're after is deeper than just trading, something beyond liquidity. Yeah, they seem willing to undertake this process just to maximize their number of retail shareholders. Maybe for branding, maybe for a better customer engagement, or maybe even for the subtle governance effects that come from having millions of small engaged owners. So the share price itself, the nominal number, has become a strategic asset in the battle for attention. It seems so a fascinating intersection of finance and marketing. It really is.
